feedback.message: Not yet. That would happen without `?? 1`. The default replaces the missing height.

hints: The first box has no `height`, so `b.height` is `undefined` and `?? 1` supplies 1.
exercises.solution: For the first box, `b.height ?? 1` is 1, so the area is 2. For the second, 3 × 4 = 12. Joined with a comma: `2,12`. TypeScript insisted on handling the missing height because `height?: number` reads as `number | undefined`.

exercises.prompt: With `type ID = string | number;` and `type Note = { id: ID; text: string };`, what type is `Note["id"]`? Write it in full, without using the name `ID`.
hints: Indexed access gives the type of the property, which here is an alias.
exercises.solution: `Note["id"]` is the type of the `id` property, `ID`, which stands for `string | number`. (Assigning a value of that type to a `never` variable makes the compiler print `Type 'ID' is not assignable to type 'never'. Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'never'.`, revealing the union member by member.)

exercises.prompt: A file contains `interface Settings { theme: string }` and, further down, `interface Settings { fontSize: number }`. What happens with `const s: Settings = { theme: "dark" };`?

options.label: Error: `fontSize` is missing, because the two declarations merged into one interface with both properties
options.feedback: Yes. Interfaces with the same name in the same scope merge, so `Settings` requires both properties.

options.label: Error: `Duplicate identifier 'Settings'`
options.feedback: Not yet. That's what two `type Settings = ...` aliases would give. Interfaces merge instead.

options.label: It compiles: the second declaration replaces the first, and `theme` is an excess property
options.feedback: Not yet. Later interface declarations don't replace earlier ones; they add to them.

options.label: It compiles: only the first declaration counts
options.feedback: Not yet. Both declarations count; they combine.

hints: What do two interface declarations with the same name do?
exercises.solution: The declarations **merge**, so `Settings` is `{ theme: string; fontSize: number }`, and the literal fails with `Property 'fontSize' is missing in type '{ theme: string; }' but required in type 'Settings'`. Declaration merging is what lets libraries' types be extended, and also why an accidental name clash can produce baffling errors.

exercises.prompt: What is the type of the `id` property of `{ id: string } & { id: number }`?

options.label: `never`
options.feedback: Yes. A value would have to be both a string and a number, and nothing is.

options.label: `string | number`
options.feedback: Not yet. That would be the union of the two object types' views. An intersection requires *both* types to hold at once.

options.label: `string`, because the first one wins
options.feedback: Not yet. Intersections are symmetric; neither side wins.

options.label: It's a compile error at the type's declaration
options.feedback: Not yet. That's what an interface `extends` would do. An intersection is accepted, and the conflict surfaces only when you try to create a value.

hints: An intersection requires a value to belong to both types.
exercises.solution: The property's type is `string & number`, which no value can satisfy, so it reduces to **`never`**. The error appears only at use: `const x: Both = { id: "a" }` gives `Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'never'`. Interfaces' `extends` reports such conflicts at the declaration, which is one argument for using it.

exercises.prompt: Which of these can be written **only** with a `type` alias, not with an `interface`? Choose all that apply.

options.label: `"open" | "closed"`
options.feedback: Yes. A union of literals is not an object shape, so only an alias can name it.

options.label: `[number, number]`
options.feedback: Yes. Tuple types are named with aliases (an interface can only extend an array type awkwardly).

options.label: `{ name: string; age: number }`
options.feedback: Not yet. An object shape can be an interface or an alias.

options.label: `string | null`
options.feedback: Yes. Unions with primitives need an alias.

options.label: An object type that another object type extends
options.feedback: Not yet. Interfaces handle extension well, with `extends`.

hints: Interfaces describe object shapes and nothing else.
exercises.solution: Interfaces can only describe object shapes (including callable and indexable ones). Unions, tuples and anything involving primitives need a `type` alias: (a), (b) and (d). Object shapes (c) and extension (e) work with either.

exercises.prompt: With `interface Person { readonly id: number; name: string }` and `const p: Person = { id: 1, name: "Lin" };`, which line is rejected?

options.label: `p.id = 2;`
options.feedback: Yes: `Cannot assign to 'id' because it is a read-only property`.

options.label: `p.name = "Lina";`
options.feedback: Not yet. `name` isn't marked `readonly`, so it can be reassigned.

options.label: `const q: Person = { id: 3, name: "Bo" };`
options.feedback: Not yet. Read-only properties can be set when an object is created.

options.label: `console.log(p.id);`
options.feedback: Not yet. Reading a read-only property is always allowed.

hints: `readonly` forbids reassignment after creation, nothing else.
exercises.solution: Only `p.id = 2` is rejected, with error TS2540. Read-only properties may be set in the object literal that creates the object and read at any time. The protection exists only at compile time.

exercises.prompt: In the lesson's first program, `amaka` is an `Employee`, which extends `Person` (with an optional `email`). The program prints `Object.keys(amaka).length`. What number does it print?

feedback.message: Not yet. `email` is in the type but not in the object; types don't create properties at run time.
Not yet. The method `greet` is a property of the object literal too.

hints: Count the properties written in the object literal, not those in the interfaces.
Methods written in an object literal are its own properties.
exercises.solution: The object literal has `id`, `name`, `address`, `team`, `startYear` and the method `greet`: **6** own properties. The optional `email` exists only in the type; at run time the object simply doesn't have it.
